zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the index, determines the diplomatic text, typography, and physical lineation.

lines.note: Kirikudaki means breaking or chopping into small pieces; the Portuguese describes reducing something to fragments by cutting. The abbreviated principal forms and the absence of a final printed stop are retained.

runs.text: Geito que dão às Cõgatanas no corte

lines.note: Kiriha names the treatment or shape of the cutting edge of small knives. The Portuguese explanation embeds Cõgatanas, with a nasal abbreviation, rather than supplying a Japanese synonym after the headword.

runs.text: pera cortar, o que não tem commumente as Ca-

lines.note: The edge is fashioned for cutting; the gloss contrasts it with that of ordinary swords. Ca- is the printed beginning of Catanas, continued on the next physical row.

runs.text: tanas, que tem o corte direito.

lines.note: Completes Catanas and states that those swords have a straight cutting edge. This is the end of the kiriha explanation, not another entry.
Kirihanashi means separating by cutting. The scan supplies the i missing from OCR Qirfanaxi; the historical -aita principal part is retained rather than replaced by a modern -ashita ending.
Botar fora completes the alternative gloss: cutting off and casting away. The short row remains part of the preceding verb entry.
Kiriharai means clearing away by cutting. Both long-o marks are downward carons; the Portuguese deſ- continues into the next row, while the provisional st allograph in afastar is retained.
Deſ-baſtar completes the clearing gloss. Yama wo kiriharoo illustrates clearing woodland or scrub; the example retains its printed long-o form rather than being regularized to a modern citation form.
The Portuguese explicitly explains the example as cutting and clearing scrub. Its short s followed by long ſ in desbaſtar is retained as printed, without harmonizing the preceding divided occurrence.
Kirihashirakashi is making someone flee by cutting or threatening to cut. Reinspection supports r in faxiracaxi, not OCR faxitacaxi; the causative meaning is completed below.

runs.text: fugir, ou indo pera cortar fazer fugir.

lines.note: Completes fazer fugir: causing flight either by an actual cutting attack or by advancing to strike. This distinguishes the causative action from simply running away.
Kirihazushi here names offcuts or remnants. The noun entry precedes a separate verb with the same beginning; ſobe- is divided from the remainder of the Portuguese word on the next line.

runs.text: jão de pois de cortada como pedaços de pao,

lines.note: Completes ſobe-jão: pieces left over after cutting, with wood offcuts as the example. The visibly separated de pois is preserved rather than normalized to depois.
Closes the list of examples of leftover fragments. This isolated abbreviation is genuine body text and belongs with the noun kirihazushi.
The separate verb entry means missing a cutting blow. The printed abbreviated form is u, not an editorially supplied su; uita and the following example support the historical -ite inflection.
Aru hito katana wo nuite begins a fable about a man drawing his sword. The scan supports nuite, not nuire; the visibly doubled comma after Vt is retained. Vôca- begins the wolf word on the next row.

Completes vôcame wo kiroo to shita ga: he tried to cut a wolf but missed. Qirifazzuite is the historical inflected form, and vouo is the tail with the object particle, as the Portuguese below confirms.
Uchikitta completes the Japanese account of cutting the tail off. Fab. is an upright citation label; the Portuguese retelling begins with a man drawing his sword and continues across the line break.

runs.text: nhando a Catana, & querendo cortar hum lo-

lines.note: Completes deſembainhando and specifies the drawn sword and intended attack on a wolf. Catana occurs inside the Portuguese explanation; lo- continues as lobo below.

runs.text: bo, errou o golpe, & cortou lhe o rabo.

lines.note: The man missed the intended blow and cut off the wolf’s tail. This resolves the Japanese vouo above and closes the fable quotation.
Kirifusagi means blocking or obstructing. The uninterrupted headword and its voiced g agree with the following gu and aida principal forms; the OCR’s internal space is not present.
Completes caminho and lists a road or entrance as objects that can be blocked. The gloss therefore concerns obstruction, not the cutting-up sense of neighboring entries.
Kirifuse means striking or cutting something down. The Portuguese completes its result on the next row; no final period is supplied where none is printed.
Completes the result as bringing something down to the ground. The scan has lowercase chão, rather than the OCR’s capitalized Chão.
Kirigirisu is glossed simply as a cricket. The historic insect name is left as printed, without using a modern zoological classification to alter the text.

runs.text: O Morrer a ferro pelejando. Vt,

lines.note: Kirijini denotes dying by the sword in combat. The visible vowel is i, correcting OCR Qurijini, and the example introduced by italic Vt follows below.
Kirijini ni shita hito describes a person who died fighting. The example repeats the same Q-initial stem as the headword, not OCR Girijinini; mor- continues in the translation below.
Completes morreo: he died by weapons while fighting. This confirms the combat-death sense rather than death by execution or accident.
Kirimawari means cutting while going around or on all sides. The printed principal forms give the historical inflection; the Portuguese alternative continues on the next row.
Explains the surrounding motion as going around on every side. This belongs to kirimawari, before the separate transitive cutting-around entry below.
Kirimawashi means cutting around an object. The -aita form is a historical s-verb inflection, not a missing modern shi sequence.
Completes the cutting-around gloss with two Portuguese expressions for around. It does not begin a new example or entry.

runs.text: Sinal, ou lugar de ferida. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Kirime first denotes the mark or site of a wound. Item introduces a further cutting-related sense on the following physical line.

runs.text: Cortadura, ou principio de couſa cortada.

lines.note: Adds an incision or the beginning of a cut object. The definition remains literal rather than importing later figurative senses of kirime.
Kirimeguri again denotes cutting around. The headword has no genuine internal word boundary after Q; the clearly printed utta is retained despite the more familiar expected past-stem vowel.
Completes the explanation as cutting while circling. The short continuation closes kirimeguri before the following disorderly-cutting entry.
Kirimidashi describes throwing people into confusion by cutting or attacking. Em continues into baraçar below; the source has no visible terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.

runs.text: baraçar, oucortar ſem ordem por muita gẽte.

lines.note: Completes embaraçar and adds cutting indiscriminately among many people. The close printed oucortar and the nasal abbreviation in gẽte are retained instead of silently regularized.
Kirimugi is identified as a kind of thin noodle or vermicelli. The Portuguese comparison explains the food without specifying a modern recipe.

runs.text: Hum certo animal como vnicorne, ou

lines.note: Kirin is explained by comparison with a unicorn and another animal named on the next row. The entry concerns the traditional creature, not an automatically imposed modern giraffe sense.
Abada supplies the second animal comparison in the preceding definition. It remains Portuguese explanatory text rather than a Japanese headword.
Kirinagashi means cutting something and sending it away with the water. Polla begins the Portuguese directional phrase completed on the following row.
Completes the action as sending the cut material down the watercourse. The visible separation in a baixo is retained alongside the historical agoa spelling.

runs.text: Certa aruore de que ſe faz madeira

lines.note: Kiri no ki names the kiri tree. The gloss describes its timber and continues below; no scientific species name is inserted into the diplomatic text.
The timber is good and light, suitable for boxes. This functional description completes the tree entry rather than introducing another meaning of kiri.
Kiryoo denotes comeliness or excellent disposition here. Its downward caron is distinguished from a circumflex; the second gloss continues with personal qualities below.

Adds good qualities and abilities, then begins Qiriǒna fito, continued at the top of column 2. The scan supports habilidades and Qiriǒna rather than the OCR’s damaged babilities and shortened Quiôna forms.
Fito completes Qiriǒna fito from the foot of column 1: a comely, well-formed person. The scan restores the missing t in OCR fio; the Portuguese adjective continues below.

Completes apeſsoado and gives a further phrase for personal appearance. The source visibly reads cotgara, without the expected intervening o, so that printed form is retained rather than normalized to kotogara.

runs.text: boa dispoſição, ou forma de corpo.

lines.note: Explains the preceding phrase as good bodily disposition or shape. This closes the kiryoo entry that crosses the column boundary.
Kiryoku means natural strength or vigor. The initial is a single roman Q belonging to the headword, not the OCR’s separately italicized O.
Completes the capacity for doing or enduring something. The gloss covers both active exertion and endurance, rather than only muscular strength.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de trabalhar, ou fa-

lines.note: Kirikiri is an adverb for working or acting briskly. The initial Q belongs to the same word; fa- continues as fazer on the following row.

runs.text: zer alguã couſa de preßa. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the gloss as doing something quickly, then begins the example kirikiri to. The existing tilde placement in alguã is retained; Qiriqirito is a continuous Japanese form.
Shimoo completes the Japanese example of finishing promptly. The printed caron is retained, and the Portuguese explicitly gives finishing or concluding something.
Specifies that the completion is rapid. This short continuation is part of the example translation, not a separate adverb entry.
Kirikizami means mincing or cutting finely. The abbreviated nasal past form ǒda is kept; the Portuguese miu- continues as miudamente below.

runs.text: damente, como quem corta, ou apara mezi-

lines.note: Completes miudamente and compares the action to cutting or trimming medicinal materials. The divided mezi- belongs to mezinhas, not to the Japanese headword.
Completes mezinhas and closes the example list. It remains a distinct physical continuation despite containing only the end of the noun and an abbreviation.
Kirikizu is a wound from cutting. The example begins receiving such a wound; cǒmu- continues as cǒmuru on the next row, with the visible caron preserved.
Completes koomuru and translates it as receiving a wound. The separated ru is the physical continuation of the verb, not another entry.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſoar aporta quando

lines.note: Kiririto is an adverb representing the sound of a door. The printed tight aporta is retained; the circumstances of the sound are supplied below.
The door makes this sound when opened or closed. The row completes the preceding sound-symbolic explanation.
Kirisaki means tearing or cutting apart. The headword begins Qiri-, not OCR Quri-, and cor- starts the Portuguese cortando continued on the next row.
Ishoo wo kirisaku illustrates cutting or slashing garments. The scan supports Raſgar, not OCR Roſgar; the object of that Portuguese verb is completed below.
Completes the example as tearing garments by cutting. Lowercase cortando and the provisional short-s st spelling in vestidos follow the local print.

runs.text: Errar no cortar, ou cortar mal.

lines.note: Kirisonji means making a mistake in cutting or cutting badly. Only the two printed principal parts are retained; a third is not reconstructed.
Kirisute is cutting off and casting away. The scan has Qiriſute without the OCR’s extra u after Q, and retains the historical tçuru form.
Kiritachi is glossed simply as cutting. The Q is part of the continuous headword; tçu and atta are abbreviated principal forms rather than independent words.
Kiritairage means destroying or subduing by the sword. The voiced gue and the other principal parts are supported by the scan; the provisional st allograph in Destruir is not globally normalized.
Kiritate introduces cutting or wounding a crowd. Mui- continues as muita below, and the resulting dispersal is described in the following lines.

runs.text: ta gente que eſtà junta de maneira que ſe eſpa-

lines.note: Completes muita gente: the people are gathered together and are struck so that they scatter. The accent in eſtà and the divided eſpa- follow the visible print.
Completes espalhe and states that the crowd flees. Fuja corrects OCR faia. The next example, ishi wo kiritatsuru, shifts to cutting or dressing stone.
Completes Cortar and explains cutting well or shaping stones. This second example is a distinct practical sense within the kiritate entry.
Kiritaoshi means felling by cutting. The printed oita is the historical past principal part, not a spelling to modernize to oshita.
Kiritsukushi means cutting everything completely. Dei- continues in deixar; the complete headword is printed without an internal space after its initial Q.
Completes deixar nada: leaving nothing uncut. This is the exhaustive force of the preceding Japanese compound.
Kiritsuki combines cutting with a thrust or stab, as the next row explains. The large initial is an ordinary capital Q, not the OCR’s lowercase q.

runs.text: ferir de ponta, ou dando eſtocada.

lines.note: Specifies wounding with the point or delivering a thrust. This completes the compound action begun with cortar on the preceding row.
Kiritori here means taking by force of arms. Cuni- begins the example about taking a country, rather than being an isolated entry.
Kuni wo kiritoru means conquering a realm. The object particle is separated here only by the physical line break after Cuni-; the provisional st spelling in Conquistar is retained.
Kiritooshi means cutting right through something. The scan supports Cortando, repairing OCR Crtando, and the translation continues from par- below.
Completes de parte a parte, through from one side to the other. It closes the kiritooshi entry rather than the following dividing verb.
Kiriwake means dividing something by cutting. The scan supports a continuous headword, and the Portuguese description continues with making pieces below.
Completes the result as making pieces. This short row closes the kiriwake definition.
Kiriwari means splitting or cleaving by cutting. The u and atta are the abbreviated forms actually printed, not expanded verb forms.
The entry names a kind of arrow and explicitly prefers Qirifuno ya to Qiriǔno ya. The caron over u and italic Meliùs are visible; Taca begins the Japanese explanation below.
Taka no ha de haida ya explains arrows feathered with hawk feathers. The source joins ha and the particle de as fade, and the Portuguese description continues below.
Completes the description with falcon feathers. The enlarged scan shows falcãao, including the extra a and its tilde position; it is not silently corrected to falcão.
Kiriori means breaking a long object by cutting it. The headword’s v is retained as the printed representation within the compound, with examples below.
Gives cane and bone as examples of elongated objects. The source’s oßo is retained, without converting the ligature to a modern spelling.
Kirioroshi is bringing something down by cutting. The gloss distinguishes this lowering action from the neighboring breaking and felling entries.
Kiriotoshi means knocking or cutting something down. Its historical oita principal part is preserved alongside the Portuguese result derrubar.
Kirishitagaye means subjugating through conquest. The initial is Q, not OCR C. The comma is set low at the right edge; the crop includes it and the explanation continues below.

Continues the conquest gloss. The damaged or anomalous phrase is provisionally read ſou pouir, as the visible types suggest; its intended Portuguese wording is not secure and is not replaced by a conjectural poder phrase. The separate Qiriya- at the right is the catchword, retained only in its furniture record.
